analysis.one_liner: Bans federal contractors with serious child labor law violations from getting federal contracts.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate committee approved the bill in December 2024 and put it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires companies bidding on federal contracts to disclose, under penalty of perjury-style False Claims Act liability, any child labor violations against them or their subcontractors in the past three years. Companies that disclose can negotiate corrective steps with the Labor Department; companies that hide violations, or that keep violating child labor law and refuse to fix it, go on a list of firms agencies may not hire for at least four years. It also orders a government study of how common child labor is among federal contractors and directs that civil fines collected for child labor violations go toward enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors working in or near federal supply chains, who gain an enforcement tool aimed at the companies that hire or subcontract them. Law-abiding contractors also gain a more level playing field, since violators could no longer undercut them by cutting labor costs. Taxpayers gain a guarantee that federal money does not go to companies found to have violated child labor law.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any company entering a federal contract to annually disclose whether any final administrative ruling, arbitration award, or civil judgment for a child labor violation (Fair Labor Standards Act section 12) was issued against it in the prior three years, and to pass that certification requirement down to its subcontractors and service providers.

Prohibits agencies from awarding contracts to companies or using subcontractors that reported child labor violations but failed to implement corrective measures negotiated with the Labor Department, and puts such firms through suspension and debarment proceedings that bar them from federal work for at least four years.

Makes knowingly false or missing child labor disclosures subject to False Claims Act penalties (sections 3729-3733 of title 31), the same statute used to recover money in fraud cases, with referral for suspension and debarment.
Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that civil penalties collected for child labor violations are available for enforcement purposes, rather than being deposited as general sums.
Directs the Comptroller General to study the prevalence of child labor violations among federal contractors and report the findings to Congress within two years.
Requires annual public reports to Congress listing how many firms were debarred, how many agreed to corrective measures, and the dollar value of their contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors and their subcontractors, especially in sectors where child labor violations have been found, such as food processing sanitation and agriculture, which would face new annual disclosure requirements, negotiated corrective measures, and possible four-year-plus bans from federal work if they cannot show compliance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal contractors with child labor violations

drawbacks.text: The disclosure requirement is built on self-reporting: companies disclose violations only 'to the best of the knowledge of the entity,' so a contractor that never asks its subcontractors can plausibly answer no, weakening the enforcement mechanism the bill relies on.

The bill authorizes no additional funds (Section 6), so the Labor Department and contracting agencies must run the new certification, negotiation, and debarment machinery within existing budgets, which could slow implementation.

A contractor's liability can be triggered by a subcontractor's violations, and the penalty for failing to disclose is a False Claims Act case plus debarment, which compliance officers could argue is a disproportionate hammer for a paperwork lapse in a large supply chain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is modest compliance paperwork for contractors against a real remedy for a documented problem: companies in federal supply chains employing minors. The bill's own design softens the blow, since firms that disclose and negotiate corrective measures stay eligible; only repeat or uncorrected violations cost them federal work. The weaknesses are the reliance on self-certification and the absence of new funding, which make the law easier to evade than its text suggests, but the burden it imposes is small compared with what violators would face.

outcome.mechanism: The Homeland Security committee approved it unanimously-style with an amendment in December 2024 and put it on the Senate calendar, but no senator ever brought it to a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so it died on the calendar.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on October 26, 2023, joined by Republican Senator Josh Hawley, and it was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on March 6, 2024, and Chairman Gary Peters formally reported it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on December 12, 2024, with written report 118-289.
The reported version was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 695 on December 12, 2024, which is where a bill waits for a floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died on the calendar with bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report.

The committee substantially rewrote the bill: the introduced version created a criminal penalty for failing to disclose, treated the full contract value as the 'gross loss to the Government' for sentencing, and imposed a fixed five-year ineligibility list prepared by the Labor Secretary; the reported version replaced the criminal penalty with False Claims Act liability and debarment, tied the bar to existing suspension and debarment procedures, and added a provision redirecting collected child labor civil penalties toward enforcement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors, including those found to have violated child labor law, kept uninterrupted access to federal contracts with no new disclosure or debarment requirements; minors working in those supply chains gained no new protection.

industries.industry: Federal contractors with child labor violations (e.g., sanitation and staffing firms in meat and food processing)
industries.note: These firms would have to disclose child labor judgments annually, negotiate corrective measures, and face a four-year-plus debarment from federal work if they keep violating; their business interest in continued contract eligibility runs directly against protecting the minors they hire.
Contractors that already follow child labor law gain a more level playing field, since competitors could no longer win federal work in part by using under-age labor.

All contractors face new annual certifications that cascade down to subcontractors and False Claims Act exposure for false disclosures, but only firms with uncorrected violations risk losing eligibility.
